chunks: "The short version is that integration wins on size, power, performance and per-unit cost at volume, and loses on flexibility, upfront cost and risk.
Power and speed come from keeping signals on the die.
A wire on chip is short and low capacitance, so moving a bit costs a fraction of what it costs to drive it through package pins and across a board, and the bus can be much wider and lower latency.
Size and BOM are obvious: one package instead of several, fewer decoupling caps, fewer layers and connectors, simpler assembly and often better reliability because there are fewer solder joints.
The costs: if you design the SoC yourself, the NRE is huge, masks, IP licenses, verification and a possible respin, so it only makes sense above a break-even volume.
A board of off-the-shelf parts is quick to build, and you can swap one chip, upgrade the memory, or second-source.
Also in a SoC everything shares one process, which isn't optimal for analog, RF or DRAM, and everything shares one heat spot.
So my rule: for high volume and tight power or size limits, integrate; for low volume, fast schedule or uncertain requirements, use catalog parts or a module.
Most teams don't design the SoC, they buy one."
